issues.failure_explanation: The space C on which J is defined requires phi(:,t) to lie in Diff_vol(Omega) for every t. By the paper's own identity (change:variables), valid because phi has unit Jacobian, the potential term satisfies integral over Omega of V(phi(X,t)) dX = integral over Omega of V dx for every volume-preserving phi; it is therefore constant on C, so its first variation along genuine C-variations is identically zero. Moreover, variations of phi within C have the form dphi = eta composed with phi with eta divergence-free, so vanishing of the dphi-pairing for all admissible dphi only forces the dphi-coefficient to be a gradient, not zero. The proof of Theorem 1 nevertheless differentiates the potential term (the displayed term '+ <grad V o phi, dphi>' vanishes on C) and applies the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations as if dphi were arbitrary, i.e., it varies phi in a larger space in which volume preservation is not imposed. Hence (necessary:conditions) is not a necessary condition for criticality of J on the declared C. Counterexample from the paper's own definitions: if phi_T = phi_0 and V is nonconstant (e.g., the obstacle potential in the Remark), the rest state (phi = phi_0, v = 0, pi = 0, k = 0) lies in C and is a critical point of J on C (the potential term is constant on C and every other term vanishes to first order), yet it violates the third equation of (necessary:conditions), which would require grad V composed with phi_0 to vanish identically. Theorem 2, whose hypothesis is criticality of J, is consequently not established as stated either.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Redefine C without the condition phi(:,t) in Diff_vol(Omega) (volume preservation then follows dynamically from div v = 0, d phi/dt = v composed with phi, and phi_0 volume-preserving), noting that identity (change:variables) is then invoked only at the base curve, which is volume-preserving at critical points. Together with the sign repair of ISSUE-002, the proofs of Theorems 1 and 2 then go through for the relaxed space.
issues.overall_effect: As written, Theorem 1's optimality system is not a necessary condition for critical points of J on the constraint space actually defined in the source, and Theorem 2's conclusion is not derived from its stated hypothesis; the chain from the optimal control problem of Section 2.4 to the modified Euler equation is broken as written.
issues.title: Theorem 1's necessary conditions are not the critical-point equations of J on the declared constraint space C (the potential term is constant on C; the proof uses inadmissible variations)
issues.why_classification: Both main theorems are false as stated for the declared constraint space (an explicit counterexample, the rest state with phi_T = phi_0 and nonconstant V, follows from the paper's own definitions), which exceeds a routine slip; however, a supported local repair - dropping the dynamically redundant volume-preservation clause from C, with a contained justification - restores both results without new proof architecture or loss of scope, so the issue is not serious.

issues.failure_explanation: The sign of the potential term is internally inconsistent. The cost (first:functional) is (1/2)<v,v> + integral of V composed with phi, and in J the kinetic term enters as -(1/2)<v,v> (the 'minus the cost' multiplier convention, calibrated by the V = 0 case, which reproduces the impulse equations), but the potential term of J is printed as +<V composed with phi>, i.e., with the opposite convention. With J as printed, the proof's own computation yields the dphi-coefficient '(Tv o phi)^T pi + d pi/dt + grad V o phi', hence d pi/dt = -(Tv o phi)^T pi - grad V o phi, and Theorem 2's argument would then produce -grad(p + V). Theorem 1 instead states d pi/dt = -(Tv o phi)^T pi + grad V o phi, and Theorem 2 states -grad(p - V) - the signs corresponding to the augmented functional with -<V composed with phi>. The proof of Theorem 1 is thus self-contradictory: its final conclusion ('Thus, again by the fundamental theorem of calculus of variations, we conclude that ...') contradicts its immediately preceding display. Therefore, for critical points of J as defined, the third equation of (necessary:conditions) and equation (mod:eulereq) are false as printed; at least one of {J, Theorem 1, Theorem 2} must be corrected.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Adopt one sign convention consistently. Least invasive: print the potential term of J as -<V composed with phi>, matching the -(1/2)<v,v> convention (augmented functional = minus the full cost of first:functional), and flip the two corresponding grad V signs in the displays of Theorem 1's proof; Theorems 1 and 2 and (mod:eulereq) then hold exactly as printed. Alternatively, keep J and flip the sign in Theorem 1's third equation and propagate through Theorem 2, obtaining -grad(p + V).
issues.overall_effect: As printed, the stated optimality system (third equation of necessary:conditions) and the central modified Euler equation (mod:eulereq) do not hold for critical points of J as defined; the proof of Theorem 1 contains an invalid final deduction; the sign of the potential's contribution to the central equation is indeterminate in the source.
issues.title: Inconsistent sign of the potential term between the augmented functional J and Theorems 1-2; the proof of Theorem 1 contradicts its own preceding display
issues.why_classification: The least severe complete resolution supported by the source is a local sign correction on the J side (three sign flips) under which every stated result holds exactly as printed; no substantive claim, guarantee, or scope is lost, and no new lemma, construction, or replacement argument is needed once the sign convention (already fixed by the -(1/2)<v,v> term) is recognized.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: This ensures that  such an optimal trajectory does not intersect $S$.
adding a potential function playing the role of a barrier function in the corresponding optimal control problem
It is interesting to note that, from the physical point of view, imposing an artificial potential in the fluid context is equivalent to generating a desired pressure.

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims the artificial potential produces obstacle avoidance: the abstract advertises 'a potential function playing the role of a barrier function' and 'Simulation results for the obstacle avoidance task', the Remark asserts 'This ensures that such an optimal trajectory does not intersect S', and Section 4 claims to show 'how the artificial potential can help the fluid avoid a circular obstacle'. The formal content establishes only that extremals satisfy a modified Euler equation in which V shifts the pressure; no avoidance mechanism is proved, and in fact V is inert in this incompressible setting: (i) by the paper's own identity (change:variables), for volume-preserving phi the potential term of the cost (first:functional) satisfies integral of V(phi(X,t)) dX = integral of V dx, the same constant for every admissible flow, so the posed optimal control problem is exactly the classical minimal-kinetic-energy problem and cannot prefer obstacle-avoiding flows - nothing forces optimal trajectories away from S; (ii) the modified Euler equation (mod:eulereq), dv/dt + v.grad v = -grad(p - V) (equally -grad(p + V) after the sign repair), with div v = 0, is equivalent to the classical Euler equation via the pressure shift q = p -/+ V, since a gradient (conservative) force is absorbed into the pressure of an incompressible flow; the velocity field and particle trajectories are therefore identical to Euler's and unaffected by V. The paper itself concedes the effect is only 'equivalent to generating a desired pressure'. The difference between the prose and the formal content is thus the entire obstacle-avoidance guarantee, which is not delivered; the simulations, integrating an Euler-equivalent equation, cannot demonstrate avoidance caused by the potential.

failure_location.quote: we show how the artificial potential can help the fluid avoid a circular obstacle located at a single point, for which no physical barrier exists

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a repair must either reformulate the cost so the potential is not invariant under volume-preserving rearrangement (e.g., acting on tagged or weighted particle trajectories instead of the integral of V composed with phi) and redevelop the theory, or withdraw the obstacle-avoidance claims, retaining only the statement that the potential redefines the pressure (p -> p -/+ V) with no dynamical effect.
issues.overall_effect: The paper's central advertised capability - obstacle avoidance (barrier behavior) for incompressible ideal flow via an artificial potential - is not delivered by any part of the formal development; the avoidance claims of the abstract, Section 2.4, the Remark, Section 4, and the interpretation of the simulation results are unreliable.
issues.title: Obstacle-avoidance claims are unsupported: the artificial potential is mathematically inert (its cost contribution is constant on volume-preserving flows, and the modified Euler equation is equivalent to Euler)
issues.why_classification: Every resolution within the present framework abandons the central promise: the potential provably affects neither the optimization (its cost contribution is constant on the admissible set) nor the dynamics (the modified Euler equation is equivalent to Euler), so no comparable obstacle-avoidance claim survives without an essentially new formulation.
